title: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA): An Ophthalmic Perspective
summary: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA), formerly Wegener's, is a rare, severe, systemic ANCA-associated vasculitis. It involves necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and systemic vasculitis, potentially affecting multiple organs, including the eyes. This poster details its comprehensive ophthalmologic and systemic features, diagnostic approach, and evidence-based management, crucial for timely intervention and preservation of vision and life.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA), formerly known as Wegener's Granulomatosis, is a severe, chronic, multisystem autoimmune disease characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the upper and lower respiratory tracts, systemic vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels, and glomerulonephritis. It is one of the Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitides (AAVs), primarily associated with PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA). Ocular involvement is common and can range from mild conjunctivitis to severe scleritis, orbital masses, and retinal vasculitis, often reflecting systemic disease activity.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology
content: Incidence: Approximately 10-20 cases per million per year.
Prevalence: Estimated 100-200 cases per million.
Demographics: Affects males and females equally; typical onset between 40-60 years of age.
Ethnicity: Predominantly affects Caucasians.
Risk Factors: Genetic predisposition (e.g., HLA-DPB1*0401), environmental triggers (e.g., silica exposure), and infections (e.g., chronic nasal carriage of Staphylococcus aureus).

branches: Environmental Triggers (Infections like S. aureus, Silica, Drugs)
ANCA-Neutrophil Interaction (ANCA binds to PR3/MPO on activated neutrophils)
Neutrophil Degranulation & NETosis (Release of cytotoxic enzymes, reactive oxygen species, neutrophil extracellular traps - NETs)
Endothelial Cell Damage (Vasculitis - small to medium vessels)
Granuloma Formation (T-cell mediated, characteristic necrotizing granulomas)

rows: Predominantly upper/lower respiratory tracts, eyes, skin. No significant renal or life-threatening involvement.
Multisystem disease, involving kidneys, lungs, CNS, heart. Life-threatening potential.
Typically PR3-ANCA positive, but MPO-ANCA can occur.
Better long-term prognosis, but can progress to generalized form.

sections.title: 5. Systemic Clinical Features
content: Constitutional: Fever, malaise, weight loss, fatigue (90%).
ENT (90%): Chronic sinusitis, otitis media, epistaxis, nasal crusting, septal perforation, saddle-nose deformity, subglottic stenosis (stridor).
Pulmonary (80-90%): Cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltrates (migratory), nodules, cavities, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.
Renal (70-80%): Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (pauci-immune), hematuria, proteinuria, red blood cell casts, renal failure.
Musculoskeletal (60%): Arthralgias (non-deforming, non-erosive), myalgias.
Skin (50%): Palpable purpura, papules, nodules, vesicles, ulcers, livedo reticularis.
Neurological (20-30%): Mononeuritis multiplex, cranial neuropathies (facial, optic), peripheral neuropathy, cerebral vasculitis (rare).
Gastrointestinal (rare): Abdominal pain, GI bleeding due to vasculitis.

sections.title: 6. Ocular & Orbital Manifestations
content: Orbit (40-60% of ocular cases): Orbital mass (granulomatous pseudotumor) causing proptosis, diplopia, pain, compressive optic neuropathy (vision loss), nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO), dacryoadenitis.
Eyelids: Granulomatous inflammation, palpable nodules, erythema, edema, ptosis.
Conjunctiva: Conjunctivitis, episcleritis, pseudomembranous conjunctivitis.

Sclera (most common severe ocular involvement): Nodular scleritis, necrotizing scleritis (with or without inflammation, 'scleromalacia perforans' if progressive thinning), peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) associated with adjacent scleritis.
Cornea: Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (crescentic stromal thinning at limbus, often associated with scleritis), stromal keratitis, corneal melt, perforation.
Uvea (rare): Anterior uveitis (non-granulomatous), posterior uveitis, panuveitis.

Retina & Optic Nerve (rare but vision-threatening): Retinal vasculitis (arterial or venous occlusion, cotton wool spots, hemorrhages), optic neuropathy (ischemic or secondary to orbital compression/inflammation).

sections.title: 7. Ocular Examination Findings
content: External: Proptosis, lid edema, erythema, palpable orbital masses, saddle-nose deformity.
Lacrimal System: Epiphora (due to NLDO), palpable lacrimal gland enlargement.

Slit-lamp: Conjunctival injection, episcleral/scleral nodules (often tender), areas of scleral thinning/necrosis, peripheral corneal guttering or ulceration (PUK), anterior chamber cells/flare (if uveitis).
Fundoscopy: Retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, signs of retinal artery/vein occlusion, optic disc edema, pallor, or cupping (compressive neuropathy).
Ocular Motility: Restricted movements (from orbital inflammation, muscle infiltration).
Visual Fields: Defects from optic neuropathy or compressive lesions.

rows: c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA (80-90% sensitivity, >90% specificity); p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA (10-20% in GPA, more common in MPA)

sections.title: 10. Staging / Grading
content: Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score (BVAS): Used to quantify disease activity at presentation and monitor response to treatment. Scores range from 0 (no activity) to a maximum of 33-36 depending on version (BVAS 2003, BVAS/WG). Higher scores indicate more severe disease activity.

Five-Factor Score (FFS): A prognostic tool for ANCA-associated vasculitis. Originally developed for polyarteritis nodosa and EGPA. Factors include age > 65 years, cardiac symptoms, gastrointestinal involvement, renal insufficiency (creatinine > 1.58 mg/dL), and proteinuria > 1g/24h. The 2009 revised FFS is used for ANCA-associated vasculitis and provides prognostic information for mortality.

sections.title: 11. Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Induction Therapy (For active, severe, or organ-threatening disease, duration 3-6 months)
a. Glucocorticoids: High-dose IV Methylprednisolone (1g IV daily for 3 days) followed by oral Prednisone (1 mg/kg/day, max 60-80 mg/day) with gradual taper.
b. Immunosuppression (Choice depends on severity, PR3-ANCA vs MPO-ANCA, and local protocols):
i. Cyclophosphamide: Oral (2 mg/kg/day) or IV pulses (0.5-0.75 g/m² monthly for 3-6 months). Highly effective but toxic (myelosuppression, hemorrhagic cystitis, malignancy risk).

ii. Rituximab: 375 mg/m² IV weekly for 4 weeks (as in lymphoma protocol) OR 1g IV on day 1 and day 15 (as in RA protocol). Non-inferior to cyclophosphamide for induction in many cases (RITUXVAS trial), preferred in relapsing disease (RAVE trial).
Step 2: Maintenance Therapy (For sustained remission, duration at least 18-24 months, often longer)
a. Azathioprine: 2 mg/kg/day PO. Standard choice, monitor LFTs and CBC.
b. Methotrexate: 15-25 mg/week PO/SC. Alternative for non-organ-threatening disease or those intolerant to azathioprine, requires folic acid supplementation.
c. Mycophenolate Mofetil: 1-2g/day PO. Less effective than azathioprine for maintenance but an option for intolerance.
d. Rituximab: 500 mg IV every 6 months or 1g IV every 12 months. Increasingly used for maintenance, especially after Rituximab induction.
e. Glucocorticoids: Tapered to lowest effective dose (e.g., <5 mg/day prednisone) or discontinued.
Step 3: Adjunctive & Supportive Care
a. Prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (PJP): Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole (e.g., 80/400 mg daily or three times weekly) for patients on cyclophosphamide or high-dose corticosteroids.
b. Bone Protection: Calcium, Vitamin D, bisphosphonates for patients on long-term steroids.
c. Gastric Protection: PPIs for patients on high-dose steroids.
d. Infection Monitoring: Regular blood counts and vigilance for infections (fungal, bacterial, viral) due to immunosuppression.

sections.title: 12. Ophthalmic Surgical Techniques
content: Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR): Indicated for persistent nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO) causing epiphora, especially after systemic disease control.

Orbital Decompression: Rarely necessary in severe orbital granuloma causing compressive optic neuropathy that is unresponsive to maximal systemic medical therapy. It aims to relieve pressure on the optic nerve.

Corneal Grafting (e.g., lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty): For severe peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) leading to corneal perforation or significant stromal thinning threatening perforation. Often requires concurrent intensive systemic immunosuppression to prevent graft melt.
Enucleation/Evisceration: In rare, extreme cases of orbital destruction or painful blind eyes.

sections.title: 13. Complications & Prognosis
content: Untreated GPA: Rapidly fatal, with median survival less than 1 year, primarily due to renal failure or respiratory failure.
Treated GPA: 5-year survival rate exceeds 80%, but significant morbidity from disease activity and treatment side effects persists.
Relapse: Common, occurring in up to 50% of patients within 5 years, often triggered by reduction or cessation of immunosuppression.
End-stage Renal Disease: A major long-term complication despite treatment, requiring dialysis or transplantation.
Permanent Organ Damage: Saddle-nose deformity, hearing loss, chronic sinusitis, tracheal stenosis, pulmonary fibrosis, blindness.
Ocular Complications: Irreversible vision loss from optic neuropathy, retinal vasculitis, corneal perforation, or glaucoma secondary to orbital disease.

Treatment-related Complications: Increased risk of serious infections (PJP, viral reactivations), malignancy (e.g., bladder cancer with cyclophosphamide), osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, avascular necrosis.

sections.title: 14. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN): Acute rise in serum creatinine, hematuria, proteinuria (indicates crescentic glomerulonephritis).
Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage (DAH): Acute hemoptysis, dyspnea, sudden drop in hemoglobin (life-threatening pulmonary involvement).
New-onset Proptosis with Vision Loss or Diplopia: Suggests compressive optic neuropathy or severe orbital inflammation.
Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK) with Impending Perforation: Acute corneal melt, severe thinning.
Sudden, Severe Vision Loss: Can indicate retinal vasculitis, optic nerve ischemia, or severe orbital compression.
Severe Subglottic Stenosis: Stridor, severe dyspnea.
Acute Neurological Deficits: New cranial nerve palsies, mononeuritis multiplex, seizures.

content.explanation:
To remember key features of Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis:
C-ANCA: Predominantly c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) positive.
Renal: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
Airway: Upper (sinus, ear, nose) and Lower (lung) respiratory tract involvement.
Necrotizing: Characteristic necrotizing granulomas and vasculitis.
Keratitis: Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) is a common ocular sign.

sections.title: 16. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Early Diagnosis is Critical: GPA is a medical emergency. Delay in diagnosis and treatment significantly increases morbidity and mortality.
Multisystem Disease: Always consider systemic involvement even if ocular symptoms dominate.
PR3-ANCA is Key: While not 100% sensitive or specific, a positive PR3-ANCA in the right clinical context is highly suggestive of GPA.
Biopsy is Gold Standard: Tissue biopsy (e.g., kidney, lung, sinus, or sclera) showing necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and vasculitis confirms diagnosis.
Ocular Involvement is Diverse: Can affect almost any part of the eye, from adnexa to retina/optic nerve.
PUK + Scleritis = Vasculitis until proven otherwise: This combination is a strong indicator of systemic autoimmune disease like GPA.
Monitor for Relapse: Patients require long-term follow-up for disease activity and treatment side effects.

sections.title: 17. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content:
Significant advancements in GPA management have emerged from landmark trials:

1.  **RITUXVAS Trial (2010)**: Demonstrated that Rituximab (a B-cell depleting antibody) combined with glucocorticoids was non-inferior to cyclophosphamide for inducing remission in new or relapsing severe ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV), particularly for MPO-ANCA positive patients.
2.  **RAVE Trial (2010)**: Confirmed that Rituximab was as effective as daily oral cyclophosphamide for induction of remission in newly diagnosed or relapsing AAV, and superior to cyclophosphamide for relapse induction, especially in PR3-ANCA positive patients.
3.  **MAINRITSAN Trials (MAINRITSAN, MAINRITSAN2, MAINRITSAN3)**: Established Rituximab as a superior maintenance therapy compared to azathioprine for preventing relapses in AAV, with a favorable safety profile. They also refined dosing and duration strategies for Rituximab maintenance.
4.  **PEXIVAS Trial (2020)**: Showed that plasma exchange (PLEX) did not significantly reduce the incidence of death or end-stage kidney disease in severe AAV when added to standard immunosuppressive therapy, challenging its routine use, except possibly in very severe cases with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.
5.  **Avacopan (C5a Receptor Inhibitor)**: The ADVOCATE trial (2021) demonstrated that avacopan, an oral selective C5aR inhibitor, was non-inferior to prednisone for inducing and maintaining remission, while allowing for significant reduction or elimination of glucocorticoid use, thereby reducing steroid-related toxicities. It is now approved as an adjunctive treatment for severe active AAV.

sections.title: 18. Pediatric & Special Population Considerations
content: Pediatric GPA: Extremely rare in children (<5% of all cases). Presentation can be more fulminant or atypical, making diagnosis challenging. Long-term immunosuppression requires careful consideration of growth, development, and fertility.

Pregnancy: GPA in pregnancy is rare. There is an increased risk of flares during pregnancy and postpartum. Management involves balancing disease control with fetal safety. Cyclophosphamide is contraindicated due to teratogenicity; azathioprine, prednisone, and rituximab (second and third trimester) are often used with careful monitoring.
Elderly Patients: May have more comorbidities, requiring careful dose adjustments of immunosuppressants and increased vigilance for infections and drug toxicities.
